RELAYFUNDS.ORG  ·  BUILT AND DEPLOYED · ONE CONTRIBUTOR · LOOKING FOR PEOPLE, NOT MONEY

Infrastructure for solidarity, built to be useless to anyone who seizes it.

Relay connects local mutual aid groups to the funds that back them, and lets people ask those groups for help without leaving a trail. It never decides who deserves aid and never touches distribution.

Encrypted  so only the group can read it No accounts  for individuals AGPL-3.0 EN / ES
Who this is for

Eleven neighbours and a spreadsheet.

They know who on their block is behind on rent, whose power is about to be cut, which family stopped answering the door. They are good at the part that is hard to systematise.

What they do not have is a way to reach the fund that would cover it - without already knowing somebody who knows somebody. So the money sits in one place and the knowledge sits in another.

The unit of trust is the group

Relay works at group level and nowhere else. Groups are accountable for the money, groups make every distribution decision, groups hold the local relationships. Relay's whole job is to stop the introduction being a prerequisite.

That is also why it can afford to know nothing about the people receiving aid.

The pattern above is drawn from docs/problem_brief.md and is illustrative of the groups Relay is designed for. No group has joined yet - see slide 12.

Two coordination failures

Not a fundraising problem. A discovery and trust problem.

Money pools in one place. Local knowledge sits in another. Neither link between them is safe to cross.

Fund hubs

An organisation that raises money centrally - a solidarity fund, a bail fund, a foundation. No safe way to tell which local groups are real.

No safe
introduction

Local groups

Know exactly who needs what. Reachable only by word of mouth and DMs.

No safe
way to search

People in crisis

Will not leave a traceable record just to look for help.

The one outside signal Relay has: a sitting state legislator, approached independently, named the absence of a safe way to find local aid as her most pressing need. Unattributed here until she agrees to be named.

Both failures fall hardest on the people with the most to lose: undocumented residents, people fleeing violence, anyone for whom a database row is a risk.

Why now

The risk here is not hypothetical. Organizers are being prosecuted.

Charity fraud and money laundering charges

Three Atlanta Solidarity Fund organizers were arrested in May 2023 over what Nonprofit Quarterly describes as routine nonprofit reimbursements. The money laundering charges were dropped in September 2024; racketeering charges under a 61-defendant RICO indictment remain outstanding.

Payment rails are a surveillance layer

IRS reporting thresholds on money-sharing apps put a durable record behind ordinary transfers between neighbours - the exact mechanism most mutual aid runs on today.

Co-optation is a live fear

Organizers actively worry that philanthropic structure and compliance requirements defang the work. Any tool entering this space is read against that suspicion, and should be.

The sector's own recommendations to mutual aid funds include decentralised organizing to reduce surveillance vulnerability, and parallel structures where visibility is a risk.

Nonprofit Quarterly, "Protecting Solidarity: Countering Attacks on Mutual Aid Funds" · Relay's design brief, arrived at independently
Why this is hard to build

Every obvious solution makes people less safe.

A directory that logs searches. An intake form that stores a phone number. An analytics tag recording who visited. Each is standard practice, and each manufactures a record that can be leaked, scraped, or lawfully demanded.

Assume seizure

The premise is that the database will one day be read by someone hostile. Not that it might be - that it will.

Minimise, do not protect

Data never collected cannot be leaked. Relay holds no individual records to secure in the first place.

Verify without paperwork

A fund hub approves them, another group vouches for them, or an established organisation refers them. Three light paths. No IDs, no rosters, no documents.

Scope, stated narrowly on purpose

A thin layer between funds and groups. Nothing more.

ISA public directory of verified groups, browsable with no account and no tracking ISA funding request workflow between groups and hubs, at group level only ISAn anonymous, end-to-end encrypted way to ask local groups for help NOTAn arbiter of who deserves aid - Relay makes no eligibility decision, ever NOTAnywhere in the distribution path - money and aid never pass through it NOTA case management or benefits system NOTA database of people who needed help
Theory of change

Remove the introduction requirement, and the existing system works better.

Activities

A verified public directory of groups.

A group-level funding request and payout workflow.

Encrypted anonymous help requests routed to matching groups.

Outputs

Groups reach hubs without a personal introduction.

Hubs vet groups without collecting sensitive documents.

People reach groups without creating a traceable record.

Outcomes

More groups connected to funds, and funds moving faster.

Aid reaches people who currently go without because searching for it is itself a risk.

Nothing new created that could be used to watch people.

Relay changes nothing about how groups do their work or who they help. It only changes how they find each other, which is why the theory is short.

How groups get funded

Groups get funded without knowing the right person.

01 · JOIN

A group registers with a name that may be a pseudonym, a service area, aid categories, and a contact address - a shared team one is what groups are asked for. Nothing else.

02 · VERIFY

A fund hub approves, another group vouches, or an established organisation refers. No documents at any point.

03 · REQUEST

An amount, a category, a region. Justification is optional and warns against personal detail.

04 · TRACK

Submitted, approved, funds sent, acknowledged. No receipts, no narratives, no recipient data.

Hubs get totals by category, groups supported, and time to funding. A per-person figure is not withheld - it cannot be produced, because the data to produce it is never collected.

How someone asks for help · the hard one

Someone asks for help, and Relay never learns who they are.

One lockbox. One key, copied and padlocked once per group. Relay holds all of it and can open none of it.

ON THEIR DEVICE

Sealed in the browser. One copy of the key is locked for each group serving the area.

ON THE SERVER

Relay holds what it cannot open. No account, no cookie, no IP on this route.

ON THE GROUP'S DEVICE

The group passphrase opens their copy of the key, and only theirs.

OFF RELAY ENTIRELY

They talk directly. The safe word proves the call is genuine.

TweetNaCl: secretbox for the payload, box for per-group key wrapping with a fresh ephemeral keypair each time. Group keys derive from a coordinator passphrase via PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 at 600,000 iterations, and the passphrase never leaves the browser. Cryptography independently reviewed.

The test that matters

Served with a warrant, Relay produces almost nothing.

What is there

  • Encrypted blobs nobody at Relay can open
  • A public list of groups that consented to be listed
  • Group-level funding amounts and dates
  • Coarse region and aid category per request

What is not there

  • Names, addresses, phones or emails Relay can read - contact details sit inside the encrypted message it cannot open
  • Individual accounts
  • IP addresses or cookies on anonymous routes
  • Any record of who browsed the directory
  • Any record of who received what
Deleted  requests go once confirmed, or after seven days Hashed  every credential at rest AGPL-3.0  the claims are auditable

The known limit, stated because a partner should press on it: coarse routing metadata - region and aid category - is stored in the clear so requests can be delivered at all. It is documented in the repository rather than glossed.

Not a concept

Built, deployed, and auditable.

37screens across four roles
188automated tests
10automated checks on every change
EN / ESevery screen, both languages

Live at relayfunds.org. React, Node and PostgreSQL on a single host behind Caddy. Every pull request runs lint, typecheck, both test suites, a migrations job diffing the applied schema against the definitions, container builds, dependency audit, CodeQL and Trivy.

Where it actually stands

No pilot has run. Nobody has used this yet.

The build is real and the production database holds zero records, because no group has joined yet. Nor can one be listed until a fund hub verifies it: both the public directory and the routing of encrypted requests only ever surface groups a hub has approved, so the first hub unlocks both halves at once. Saying so plainly is the point - a project asking to be trusted with other people's safety does not get to overstate itself.

Paused February 2026

Development stopped after the last planned build phase shipped, and restarted in August 2026 to repair the deployment and clear the open issues.

Single host, no alerting

One rented server, running everything. An outage earlier this year was found by hand, not by a monitor.

The nonprofit is intended, not formed

Mythic Works LLC is building Relay and means to transfer it to a 501(c)(3). That entity is not incorporated anywhere yet, which is one of the reasons this deck is not asking anyone for money.

Every limitation above is a numbered issue in the public tracker, including the uncomfortable ones. What that buys a partner: the thing you would be piloting exists today and can be examined line by line, rather than described.

The ask, concretely

One hub. Three to five groups. Thirty to forty-five days.

A partner provides: one fund hub willing to route real money through the workflow, introductions to three to five local groups, and honest feedback when it does not work.

Relay provides: the platform, onboarding, support throughout, and a facilitator. No cost to participants.

Participation is opt-in and endable by any party at any time. If it does not clearly help, it stops - written into the proposal, not implied.

What is missing

The hard part is built. What is missing is people.

The repository has one contributor. Everything on the previous slides was made by one person, which is why the engineering is the part that is finished and everything else is not.

Someone with roots in mutual aid

The thing everything else waits on, and the one part that cannot be coded around. Relationships with hubs and groups, and the standing to say to organizers that this is safe to try.

Someone to build the organisation

The 501(c)(3) is intended and not incorporated. Formation, a board, the operating and governance side. Nobody is doing this today.

Engineers

10 open issues, all public. About a third of the server code is covered by tests, the browser side only where the encryption lives, and nothing watches the site for outages.

Someone trying to break it

The cryptography has been independently reviewed once. The application around it has not, and that is where this kind of design usually fails.

This is a co-founder conversation, not a volunteer listing. The entity does not exist yet, which means what it looks like and who runs it are still genuinely open.

Nobody is asking you for money

Relay is not fundraising. Mythic Works LLC is building it and intends to transfer it to a 501(c)(3), which is not incorporated yet - and until there is a pilot worth pointing at, there is nothing worth raising against.

The AGPL-3.0 licence already makes the give-away partly irreversible: the code cannot be closed by anyone, including its current owner.

What you would be joining

Real code, deployed, open, and reviewed. No users, no revenue, no staff, and a nonprofit that has not been formed. A single small server and the builder's time is the entire cost base, carried directly.

Everything about the organisation is still open, which is the argument for coming in now rather than later.
